findings.F1: The book loses on every coin, before fees as well as after. Mean daily return is -4.4 to -13.3 bps and Sharpe -0.32 to -0.92. The mean trade earns -0.08 % to -0.52 % before fees and -0.18 % to -0.62 % after, against a cost of 0.19 % per round trip. The median trade lasts 8 hours.
findings.F2: The loss comes from the shorts taken after rises. Trades with |entry forecast| above 2 earn +0.29 % to +0.80 % before fees when long. When short they lose -0.60 % to -1.16 % (34,781 trades with |forecast| above 10).
findings.F3: In high volatility (24-hour volatility at or above its 720-bar average), a 2-hour fall of at least 2 usual moves is followed by a large unusual rise. It is +60 bps over 8 hours (t 4.4, n 1,361), +172 bps over 24 hours (t 4.8, n 447) and +180 bps over 48 hours (t 3.0, n 218). The same-sized 2-hour rise is followed by only +21 bps of decline over 8 hours (t 1.9), +14 bps over 24 hours (t 0.5) and a 141 bps continuation over 72 hours (t -1.8).
findings.F4: The reversal is graded by the size of the 2-hour fall, and only the larger falls clear the 19 bps cost. On the 8-hour grid, in high volatility, the unusual move counted in both directions is 3.5 bps for |z| up to 1 (n 11,421) and 17 bps for 1 to 2 (n 4,477). It rises to 32, 50, 53 and 68 bps for 2–3, 3–4, 4–6 and above 6. After falls alone, over 24 hours, it is 7, 36, 87, 222 and 541 bps (t 3.5 in the top bin).
findings.F5: The reversal is also graded by how high volatility is against its average. For 2-hour moves of at least 2 usual moves, the 8-hour unusual move is -41 and -28 bps where the ratio is below 1.0. It is -6 bps at a ratio of 1.0–1.3, then 45, 67 and 92 bps at 1.3–1.7, 1.7–2.5 and above 2.5 (t 2.8, 3.6 and 2.8). Over 24 hours it reaches 163 bps at 1.7–2.5 (t 3.5).
findings.F6: The book's trading is mostly in cases too small to pay. Its position earns 0.12 bps per bar before costs, against about 0.46 bps of estimated turnover cost. Bars with |forecast| between 0.5 and 10 lose -0.31 to -0.52 bps each.
findings.F7: A 24-hour fall in high volatility carries the same graded rebound over the next 24 hours. It is +74 bps (t 4.0, n 994) for 1 to 2 usual 24-hour moves, +124 bps (t 4.0) for 2 to 3 and +308 bps (t 3.5) beyond.
findings.F8: The after-fall rebound over 24 hours holds in both halves of the windows. It is +82 bps in w1–12 (t 1.7, n 199) and +244 bps in w13–24 (t 4.7, n 248). By coin, the 24-hour moves after both directions are positive in 5 of 6 coins, with LTC the exception.

ideas.idea: A coin's large 2-hour fall, made while its 24-hour volatility is high, is followed by a rise over the next 24 hours, at any hour of the day. The larger the fall against the coin's usual 2-hour move, and the higher its 24-hour volatility against its 30-day average, the larger the rise.
ideas.consequence: A trader buys sharp falls in volatile markets and holds about a day, instead of also shorting sharp rises, which keep going and carry the book's losses.
ideas.name: volatile two-hour fall rebounds

ideas.idea: A coin's fall over the past 24 hours, made while its 24-hour volatility is high against its 30-day average, is followed by a rise over the next 24 hours. The larger the fall against the coin's usual 24-hour move, the larger the rise.
ideas.consequence: A slower one-day capitulation signal gives fewer, larger rebounds per trade, well above a round trip's cost.
ideas.name: volatile daily fall rebounds

ideas.idea: A coin's large 2-hour rise, made while its 24-hour volatility is high, is followed by a further rise over the next 3 days. The larger the rise against the coin's usual 2-hour move, the larger the further rise.
ideas.consequence: If confirmed, it is a reason never to short sharp rises in volatile markets, and possibly to follow them.
ideas.name: volatile two-hour rise continues
